title: Technopaegnion
author: Decimus Magnus Ausonius
source: Translated by Claude from stoa0045.stoa028.perseus-lat2, as held by the Perseus Digital Library.

passages.original: Ausonius Pacato Proconsuli Scio mihi aput alios pro laboris modulo laudem non posse procedere, quam tamen si tu indulseris, ut ait Afranius in Thaide: maiorem laudem quam laborem invenero. quae lecturus es monosyllaba sunt, quasi quaedam puncta sermonum: in quibus nullus facundiae locus est, sensuum nulla conceptio, propositio, redditio, conclusio aliaque sophistica, quae in uno versu esse non possunt: set cohaerent ita, ut circuli catenarum separati, et simul ludicrum opusculum texui, ordiri maiuscula solitus: set in tenui labor, at non tenuis gloria, si probantur.
passages.english: Ausonius to Pacatus the proconsul. I know that among others I cannot win praise in proportion to the small measure of my labour; yet if you grant it, then, as Afranius says in the Thais, "I shall have found more praise than labour." What you are about to read are monosyllables, like certain dots of speech: in them there is no room for eloquence, no conception of ideas, no proposition, response, conclusion, and the other devices of the sophists, which cannot exist within a single line; but they hold together in such a way as the rings of chains, though separate, [hold together], and at the same time I have woven a playful little work, I who am accustomed to begin larger things. But "the labour is in slight things, yet the glory is not slight," if they are approved.
passages.notes: "in tenui labor, at non tenuis gloria" echoes Virgil, Georgics 4.6. "et simul" is awkward and may be corrupt; the sense of the chain simile (separate links that nonetheless cohere) is clear. "aput" is the edition's spelling of "apud".

passages.original: Ennius ut memorat, repleat te laetificum gau.
passages.english: As Ennius records, may joy-bringing "gau" fill you.
passages.notes: "gau" is Ennius' truncated form of "gaudium" (joy), kept here because the poem ends each line in a monosyllable. This line appears to be a fragment of a longer monosyllabic sequence.

passages.original: Bucolico saepes dixit Maro, cur Cicero saeps?
passages.english: In the Bucolics Maro said *saepes* ["hedge"]; why does Cicero [say] *saeps*?
passages.notes: Maro is Virgil. The line contrasts two forms of the nominative of the word for "hedge", *saepes* and *saeps*. Like the other lines of this piece, it ends on a monosyllable. I have left the forms in Latin because the point is grammatical.
